title: Before the Storm
body:
# Before the Storm

## How the World Changes When Weather Is Coming

Lake Michigan turns green. This is the first sign, and the most reliable. Two to four hours before a major storm system arrives, the lake's surface color shifts from its usual gray-blue to a specific, unmistakable green — a desaturated jade that experienced waterfront residents read like a warning placard. The color change is caused by the storm's advance pressure wave interacting with the lake's surface biology, pushing algae and suspended particulates toward the surface where they tint the water. The science is understood. The visceral response is not scientific — it is ancient, mammalian, the part of the brain that predates language looking at a horizon that has changed color and knowing that something is coming.

The Behemoths in the wasteland know before the lake changes color. Trackers who monitor the autonomous megastructures have documented a consistent pattern: twelve to eighteen hours before a major weather event, the Behemoths alter their behavior. Their routes shift, avoiding low-lying terrain and converging on elevated positions. Their sensor arrays adjust, orienting toward the approaching system with a attentiveness that suggests they are not merely detecting the storm but studying it. One tracker described watching a Behemoth — a machine the size of a city block — turn to face an approaching supercell the way a person turns to face an old acquaintance. There was, the tracker said, recognition. Not fear. Not urgency. Recognition. The Behemoth knew this weather. The Behemoth had seen it before. The Behemoth was watching it arrive with the patience of something that has survived every storm the atmosphere has ever produced.

The animals in GLMZ respond on a shorter timeline — four to six hours before landfall. The BCI-navigating pigeons go to ground, abandoning their rooftop roosts for the deeper shelter of the Gray Zone's interior corridors. The bioluminescent cats of the Old Harbor district emerge from the Underworld tunnels and climb — upward, to the highest accessible point, as if altitude confers safety. The geneware-contaminated rats of Block 7 seal their wall-cavity nests with chewed insulation and go silent, the entire colony entering a stillness that the residents have learned to recognize as a more reliable weather forecast than the municipal service provides. The animals know. They have always known. The difference is that in 2200, some of them are augmented enough that the knowing registers on instruments.

In the city itself, the hours before a storm produce a specific human choreography. Rooftop gardens are covered with polymer sheeting secured by whatever is heavy enough to resist wind. Exterior-facing windows — the ones that still open, in the older the Gray Zone buildings that predate sealed climate control — are closed and reinforced with scavenged materials. The charging stations for augmented limbs see a surge of users, because a storm means potential power disruption, and a power disruption means your arm runs on battery, and your battery runs on what you charged it to before the grid went down. The charging stations become, in the hours before a storm, the most social places in the Gray Zone — people standing in line, chrome arm plugged into a shared outlet, watching the sky change color through the corridor windows and sharing the specific camaraderie of people preparing for something they cannot prevent and must survive.

The specific green that means a supercell has its own name in the Gray Zone. They call it "jade hour" — the period between the lake changing color and the storm making landfall, when the light in the city takes on a filtered, aquatic quality and the air pressure drops fast enough to feel in your sinuses and in the joints of your augmentations. During jade hour, the city is its most beautiful and its most dangerous — the green light flattening shadows, the wind dropping to an unnatural calm, the electromagnetic environment shifting in ways that BCI users perceive as a subtle change in the texture of their feed. Something is coming. The lake knows. The machines know. The animals know. And then the first thunder arrives, and knowing becomes experiencing, and the city hunkers down beneath a sky that has remembered it is bigger than anything humans have built beneath it.
